# geoindex — SPEC

## Maturity

**Grade:** 4 · S4 E1 A2 H3 P3 · limited by scope (mvp) *(generated by `zig build gen-catalog`)*

**Scope:** mvp — Flatbush 4.6.2 + geoflatbush 2.2.1 (surveyed 2026-09-30)

**Audit:** review 2026-08-06 · mutation 2026-10-05 (30/34, 4 eq) · src ?

**Hardening:** fuzz 2026-10-10 (200,000-run budget per harness clean, GEOINDEX_FUZZ) · ct n/a — geo index (keyword review, 2026-10-07)

**Performance:** not measured

**Evidence:** model-fuzz — Hilbert R-tree compared to naive linear-scan oracle over random point sets plus fuzz
**Model:** src/root.zig:Oracle

**Known defects:** none recorded

**Downstream consumer:** no

A frozen static spatial index for bbox + nearest-neighbour queries over a large,
fixed set of geo-points. Build from `(lat, lon, value)` triples → freeze to a
flat byte buffer → query that buffer zero-copy from a read-only / mmap'd slice.
See `README.md` for the module purpose and the usage-facing contracts.

**Where we are ahead:** the only Zig frozen, zero-copy (mmap-able), versioned and checksummed spatial index found; bounded work (`max_visited`) with truncated-prefix semantics so an attacker query cannot walk the set; no query-side allocation; exact f64 round trip; tested against a linear-scan oracle including pole/antimeridian extremes and against a corrupt-buffer fuzz harness. **Where we are behind:** no max-distance cap on `knn` itself (`within` is the radius query), payload `u32` only. Built since the survey: rectangle items (`Builder.addBox`), great-circle (haversine, metres) `knn` and `within`, the antimeridian-aware planar metric, a clamped build-time fan-out.

## Design decision — packed Hilbert R-tree vs Z-order array vs grid

**Chosen: a packed Hilbert R-tree, bulk-loaded bottom-up and frozen to a flat
array of fixed-size node records (the Flatbush lineage).**

The set is *static*, so there is no insert/rebalance cost to amortize — the whole
tree is bulk-loaded once. Points are sorted along a 16-bit Hilbert space-filling
curve (spatial locality: points close in space are close in the array), then
packed bottom-up: `fanout` consecutive leaves group into one internal node whose
box is their union, repeated level by level up to a single root. Emitting leaves
first and the root last yields the key structural invariant below.

Why this over the two alternatives the brief offered:

- **vs a Z-order / geohash sorted array (range-scan + refine).** A Morton/geohash
  array answers bbox as one or more contiguous index ranges, but a query
  rectangle maps to *many* disjoint Z-ranges (the curve re-enters the rectangle
  repeatedly), so you either over-scan or maintain a range list; kNN needs an
  expanding-ring refinement that is fiddly to bound. An R-tree gives a single
  tree with real per-node bounding boxes → tight bbox pruning and a clean
  best-first kNN, at a modest ~1/15 internal-node overhead.
- **vs a uniform / adaptive grid.** A grid is excellent for uniformly dense data
  but degrades badly on the *clustered* distribution real addresses have (dense
  cities, empty countryside): a fixed cell size is either too coarse for cities
  or explodes cell count for the countryside. The R-tree adapts to density for
  free.

The decisive tie-breaker is the frozen-buffer threat model (below): the R-tree's
bottom-up layout gives a **strictly-decreasing child-index invariant** that makes
traversal termination provable on an untrusted buffer with a single comparison —
the same robustness lever the sibling `trie` module leans on. A Z-order array
would lean on `binary-search + range` bounds instead; workable, but the R-tree's
monotone-index proof is simpler to audit.

Refinements the reference does not have (STR bulk-load, fixed-point coordinates, an out-of-core build) are named in *What is deliberately not done*.

### Cost model

- **Memory (frozen):** header 40 B + `node_count` × 39 B. `node_count ≈
  item_count × fanout/(fanout−1) ≈ 1.07 × item_count` at the default `fanout = 16` (`Builder.fanout`, clamped to 2..65535 as Flatbush clamps its `nodeSize`; a wider fan-out is fewer, bigger nodes) → ~42 B
  per point.
- **Build:** O(N log N) — dominated by the Hilbert sort; the pack is O(N). Held in
  a few growable arrays (point pool + node pool), a handful of allocations total.
- **`bbox`:** O(hits + visited internal nodes), bounded by `max_visited`. Zero
  allocation (caller result buffer + a fixed inline DFS stack).
- **`knn`:** O((k + visited) · log(heap)), bounded by `max_visited`. Zero
  allocation (caller-supplied heap scratch).

## Frozen wire format (version 1)

All integers **little-endian**; each `f64` is stored as its IEEE-754 `u64` bit
pattern, also little-endian. The buffer is `header ++ node_region`.

### Header — 40 bytes at offset 0

| off | size | field | meaning |
|----:|-----:|-------|---------|
| 0  | 4 | `magic`         | ASCII `"ZGI1"` |
| 4  | 2 | `version`       | format version = 1 |
| 6  | 2 | `endian_marker` | `0x0102` — detects a wrong-endian / garbage load |
| 8  | 4 | `flags`         | bit 0 = at least one leaf is a rectangle (`Builder.addBox`; informational, a leaf record carries its own box); the rest reserved, 0 |
| 12 | 4 | `node_count`    | number of node records |
| 16 | 2 | `node_bytes`    | record stride = 39 (validated on load) |
| 18 | 2 | `fanout`        | build-time R-tree fan-out, 2..65535 (informational) |
| 20 | 8 | `item_count`    | number of indexed items (points and rectangles) |
| 28 | 4 | `root_index`    | index of the root node record |
| 32 | 4 | `body_crc`      | CRC-32 of the node region (checked by `loadVerified`) |
| 36 | 4 | `header_crc`    | CRC-32 of bytes `[0..36)` |

`Header.load` validates magic, header CRC, endian marker, version, the record
stride, and the mutual consistency of `item_count` / `node_count` / `root_index`
(including the empty index: `item_count == 0 ⇒ node_count == 0`) — all O(1),
without scanning the body. `loadVerified` additionally checks `body_crc`.

### Node region — starts at offset 40

A contiguous array of `node_count` fixed-size records (stride 39). The tree is
packed **bottom-up**: leaf records first (indices `[0, item_count)`), then each
internal level, and the **root last**. **Invariant:** every child of a node has a
**strictly smaller index** than the node, and a node's children occupy a
contiguous block entirely below it. The decoder enforces `child_index <
parent_index`; because followed indices strictly decrease and are bounded below
by 0, traversal **provably terminates even on a corrupt buffer**.

Each 39-byte record:

| off | size | field | meaning |
|----:|-----:|-------|---------|
| 0  | 1 | `flags`       | bit0 = leaf (record is a single indexed item: a point, or a rectangle) |
| 1  | 8 | `min_lat`     | bounding box; for a leaf the item's own: `min == max == the point`, or a rectangle's corners |
| 9  | 8 | `min_lon`     | |
| 17 | 8 | `max_lat`     | |
| 25 | 8 | `max_lon`     | |
| 33 | 4 | `data`        | leaf: stored `value`; internal: `child_start` (index of first child) |
| 37 | 2 | `child_count` | internal: number of contiguous children; leaf: 0 |

## Coordinate & precision decisions

- **f64, not fixed-point.** WGS84 degrees in f64 carry ~15 significant digits
  (sub-millimetre); storing points as-is means the index returns coordinates
  **byte-identical** to the input, so the differential oracle can compare exact
  bit patterns and there is no quantization error to reason about. Fixed-point
  (e.g. int32 micro-degrees) would halve the box storage but reintroduce
  rounding at cell edges and a lossy round-trip; deferred, not needed at RÚIAN
  scale.
- **Ranges:** `lat ∈ [-90, 90]`, `lon ∈ [-180, 180]`, inclusive. Rejected at
  build with `error.OutOfRange`; NaN/inf with `error.NotFinite`.
- **Antimeridian.** `bbox` with `min_lon > max_lon` is a rectangle wrapping across
  ±180° and is answered as `[min_lon, 180] ∪ [-180, max_lon]` (two disjoint
  passes: no duplicates; shared output buffer, visit budget and filter; status of
  the first truncating pass). `within` and `knn` measure the longitude difference the
  short way round, in both metrics (geoflatbush does; a query at -179.95° finds a point at 179.9°
  0.15° away, not 359.85°), and the pruning bound looks at the box and the copies of it a turn of
  longitude away. A rectangle ITEM does not wrap (`addBox` refuses `min_lon > max_lon`): a footprint
  across the antimeridian is two items.
- **Rectangles (Flatbush's main case).** `Builder.addBox(min_lat, min_lon, max_lat, max_lon, value)` adds a
  rectangle (edges inclusive; `error.InvertedBox` for a minimum above its maximum); the leaf record is the
  same 39 bytes with its own box, so the format has no new field (header `flags` bit 0 says a rectangle is
  present, for tools; a reader from before rectangles reads such a leaf as a point at its minimum corner).
  Items are Hilbert-sorted by their box centre. `bbox` returns every item whose box meets the query rectangle
  (`Match.max_lat`/`max_lon` carry the extent, `isPoint()` tells the two apart); `knn` and `within` rank an
  item by the distance to the nearest point of its box, 0 inside it; a point is a degenerate box and its
  distance is computed as before (bit-identical). Spec reference: Flatbush `add(minX, minY, maxX, maxY)`,
  `search`, `neighbors`.
- **Hilbert grid.** Points are mapped into a 65536×65536 grid spanning the data's
  overall bounding box for the Hilbert sort. A zero-width axis (all points share
  a latitude/longitude) collapses to grid column/row 0 — no divide-by-zero. The
  exact Hilbert mapping affects only query *locality*, never correctness (any
  deterministic order produces a valid packed R-tree), so a clear iterative
  xy→d mapping is used rather than a bit-twiddled one.

## kNN distance metric

Best-first R-tree search over a min-heap: the heap holds pending internal nodes
(keyed by the lower-bound distance from the query point to the node's box) and
pending leaf points (keyed by the exact point distance). Popping the minimum
always yields either the next-nearest point (emit) or the nearest unexplored node
(expand) — a point can never be beaten by anything inside a farther box — so
results come out in exact ascending order and a budget cut returns a correct
prefix.

By default (`QueryOptions.metric = .planar`) the metric is an **equirectangular approximation** scaled by the
cosine of the query latitude. With `qk = cos(qlat)` and `wrap` the longitude difference taken the short way
round (into [-180, 180]):

```
dx = wrap(lon − qlon) · qk ;  dy = lat − qlat ;  dist2 = dx·dx + dy·dy
```

Because `qk` is a single constant per query, this is an anisotropic linear scaling of the (lon, lat) plane, so
the squared distance from the scaled query point to a scaled axis-aligned node rectangle is a **true lower
bound** on the distance to any point in that box (taken over the box and its copies a turn of longitude away,
so the bound holds across the antimeridian) → pruning never drops a real neighbour, and the oracle can
reproduce the identical f64 arithmetic bit-for-bit. `dist2` is a ranking key in this metric (degrees²), **not
metres**. Ties break by `(dist2, value, lat, lon)` ascending — a total order (any remaining equal keys are
identical items, so the output is deterministic).

**Great circle** (`QueryOptions.metric = .great_circle`; geoflatbush's `around`): haversine distance on a
sphere of radius 6371 km, in **metres** (`radius` in metres, `Neighbor.dist2` metres squared,
`Neighbor.dist()` the metres). Correct at any latitude, over the poles and across the antimeridian. The node
bound is the great-circle distance from the query to the rectangle: inside the rectangle's longitudes the latitude gap on
the query's meridian, else, for each of the two edge meridians, the foot of the perpendicular from the query when
it falls within the edge and the distance to its two ends otherwise (the exact distance to the box; the same
function ranks a rectangle item). Tested against a textbook haversine scan over the whole map, the poles and the
dateline, and `Ranker.box` against dense samples of the box in both metrics. The index is
bit-compared to its oracle in the planar metric; in this one results agree to rounding (a haversine
scan and the index may order two items within a millimetre either way).

## Radius and filter queries

- **`within(lat, lon, radius, out, opts)`** (kdbush `within`, geoflatbush `maxDistance`): every item whose
  distance in `opts.metric` is `<= radius`. In the default `.planar` metric the radius is in **degrees of
  latitude** (longitude difference scaled by `cos(query latitude)`), not metres; with `.great_circle` it is
  **metres**. Each result is a `Neighbor` carrying `dist2` (squared distance, `<= radius^2`); the
  order is unspecified (depth-first), sort by `dist2` if it matters. A negative or NaN radius, or NaN
  query coordinates, match nothing; radius 0 matches the items exactly at the query. Subtrees whose
  box lower bound exceeds the radius (padded by 1e-9 degrees, or 1 mm, against rounding) are pruned. Status,
  capacity and the `max_visited` budget behave as for `bbox` (`WithinStatus` is `BboxStatus`); an empty
  `out` over a non-empty index is `.truncated_capacity`. No allocation.
- **`QueryOptions.filter`** (geoflatbush `filterFn`): a `Filter{ ctx, func }` predicate over a candidate
  `Match`, applied during the search by `bbox`, `within` and `knn` (Zig has no closures, hence the
  context pointer; it must not mutate the index buffer). A rejected point is neither reported nor
  counted against the result capacity or `k`, so `knn` still returns the k nearest points that pass;
  rejecting points does not widen the visit budget.

## DoS / bounded-work model

Both queries take `QueryOptions.max_visited` (default **100 000**): the maximum
number of node records the query may decode before stopping. A bbox covering
everything, or a kNN over millions of points, cannot walk the whole set — it
stops at the budget. `bbox` reports `.truncated_budget`, or `.truncated_capacity`
if the caller's result buffer fills first (distinguishable so the caller knows
whether to enlarge the buffer or accept a partial answer). `knn` best-first emits
in exact order, so a budget cut yields a correct, merely shorter, prefix. The
inline `bbox` DFS stack is capped at `max_stack` (4096); a buffer that would
overflow it is treated as corrupt (`error.StackOverflow`). `knn`'s heap lives in
caller scratch; overflow is `error.ScratchTooSmall` (never silent dropping, which
would break exactness). `max_visited = 0` disables the budget and must not be
used on attacker-influenced queries.

## Threat model — untrusted frozen buffers

A frozen buffer may come from a file outside the process trust boundary
(truncated, bit-flipped, or hand-crafted). Guarantees:

- **Never panics, never reads out of bounds, never loops forever** on any input
  buffer. Every index the query path follows out of the buffer is bounds-checked
  in `format.zig` (`Nodes.at`, `Nodes.child`); a bad index yields a typed
  `error.Corrupt`. Child-start + child-index arithmetic is overflow-checked.
- **Header validation** rejects short buffers (`Truncated`), wrong magic
  (`BadMagic`), unknown version (`UnsupportedVersion`), wrong record stride
  (`BadNodeBytes`), wrong endian (`BadEndian`), a corrupt header
  (`HeaderCorrupt`), and an inconsistent/out-of-range root (`MalformedRoot`).
  `loadVerified` adds `BodyCorrupt` (node-region CRC).
- **Termination** rests on the strictly-decreasing bounded child-index invariant
  plus the explicit visit budget — not on trusting `child_count` or any length
  field. A corrupt `child_count` can only make individual child follows fail
  bounds/invariant checks; it can never cause an over-read or an unbounded walk.

CRC-32 is an integrity check against accidental corruption / bit-rot, **not** a
security MAC; it does not authenticate a deliberately-forged buffer. A buffer
that survives `loadVerified` is only guaranteed *safe to query* (no crash / OOB /
hang), not *trustworthy in content*. Sign the file at a higher layer if producer
authenticity matters.

## Verification

Run: `scripts/modtest geoindex`. Tests live in `src/root.zig` (oracle and controls), `src/query.zig`,
`src/format.zig`, `src/builder.zig` and `src/fuzz_test.zig`.

- **Rectangles, great circle, antimeridian, fan-out** (`src/extent_test.zig`, `Ranker` test in `query.zig`): `bbox` over mixed points and rectangles equal to a scan with the extents returned; `knn` and `within` over rectangles equal to a clamped-distance scan; the great-circle `knn` and `within` against a textbook haversine scan (and a sampled-boundary distance for rectangles) over the whole map with queries at the poles and on the dateline; a planar `knn` across ±180°; eight fan-out values (0, 1, 2, 3, 7, 16, 100, 65535) giving one answer; `Ranker.box` never above the nearest of 289 samples in the box, in both metrics, and within a stated gap of it; `addBox` refusals.
- **Differential oracle** (`Oracle` in `src/root.zig`, the card's `**Model:**` line): a naive linear-scan
  reference computes the true bbox-membership multiset and the true kNN (exact distances, identical
  metric and tie-break) and must agree exactly with the index over randomized point sets and queries:
  bbox set equal, kNN sequence, order and `dist2` equal. `within` and the filtered queries are held to
  a brute-force scan the same way, as is the antimeridian-wrapping `bbox`.
- **Adversarial sets:** empty, single point, all-identical, collinear, duplicate coordinates with
  different values, points on a bbox edge/corner, zero-area (point) bbox, `k` > set size,
  pole/antimeridian extremes, a bbox matching everything (budget/capacity paths), NaN/inf rejected at
  build, a set large enough to cross many R-tree levels.
- **Boundaries of the guards:** the exact visit-budget edge, capacity versus budget truncation, an empty
  result buffer, a node with more matching children than the DFS stack holds (`StackOverflow`), too
  small a kNN scratch (`ScratchTooSmall`), a tie between a direct-child point and a node-wrapped point.
- **Format and loader:** header round trip and both CRCs; every refusal (short, magic, version,
  endian, stride, flipped, region length, root/item/node consistency at each edge, reserved flag bits);
  `Nodes.at` at `count` and at a record one byte past the buffer; the strictly-decreasing child-index
  rule; truncated buffers of every length; the Hilbert mapping is a bijection and locality-preserving;
  freeze is deterministic and every parent box encloses its children.
- **Corrupt-buffer fuzz:** two harnesses, random bytes and mutated-valid buffers (damaged with both
  CRCs re-sealed, so the damage reaches the descent), run through `std.testing.fuzz` and through the
  deterministic driver `GEOINDEX_FUZZ=<runs>[,<first seed>]` (testkit's fuzz driver); only typed
  errors, never a panic. Reach tests assert that each harness hits every outcome, and corpus tests pin
  what the random buffers get past and that the mutation scripts reach the descent.
- **Positive controls:** a corrupted leaf value makes the index disagree with the oracle (and the body
  CRC catches it); a hand-crafted self-pointing child is rejected as `error.Corrupt`, not looped.
- **Round trip:** in-memory answers equal the answers after build, freeze and load.
- **Audit:** the card's `**Audit:**` line is the current score, cumulative over the last whole-module
  mutation run and the delta runs after it.

## Anchoring

**Anchor grade:** class C · oracle n/a

- **Class C** — internal algorithm or data structure — no outside exists, so correctness is defined by invariants or a brute-force reference. Not anchor debt.
- **Oracle n/a** — class C/D carries no anchor debt, so there is no oracle grade to give.

**What the tests actually contain.** in-process Hilbert R-tree; naive linear-scan self oracle only (SPEC.md)

## What is deliberately not done

- **STR (Sort-Tile-Recursive) bulk-load:** the reference (Flatbush) packs by Hilbert order too; STR would tile the plane
  first for slightly tighter leaf boxes. Not something a user of the reference expects, and the single-axis
  Hilbert order already gives good locality.
- **Fixed-point coordinate storage:** halves box bytes at the cost of a lossy round trip; the reference
  stores floats, and the exact f64 round trip is a feature here (unnecessary at RÚIAN scale).
- **A dense root fan-out table, SIMD node scans:** the fan-out is a build-time choice (`Builder.fanout`, 2..65535,
  recorded in the header); the decoder reads `child_count` per node. A faster scan is a measurement-led change with no
  consumer asking, and Flatbush has none.
- **An on-disk / larger-than-RAM build:** the reference builds in memory; the pack holds the node pool in memory
  before freezing. A frozen buffer is mmap-able for queries, which is where the scale is.
- **Payloads wider than `u32`:** Flatbush's payload is the item's position; callers store a `u32` record id and
  indirect through their own table (as the sibling `trie` does).
